title: Additive rule 90 only transmits randomness from its initial conditions

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Additive rule 90 only transmits randomness from its initial conditions

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because rule 90 is additive, its patterns are superpositions of the single-cell nested pattern, so it cannot generate randomness intrinsically; any randomness it shows comes from the initial conditions, and deviations such as a low initial density persist forever, unlike in rule 22.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In rule 22 the low initial density has no long-term effect. But in rule 90 its effect continues forever.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 6, “Starting from Randomness”; section “Randomness in Class 3 Systems” (from p. 261), p. 265. Scope: additive cellular automata (rule 90) versus non-additive class 3 rules (rule 22)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch06-15: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.93

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Additivity and superposition are exact algebraic facts that settle the main mechanism. Existing simulations directly test persistence of initial-density effects, though the broad randomness wording remains interpretive.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use rule 90's linearity over GF(2) to express every evolution as the XOR superposition of shifted single-cell evolutions, and derive how biased or correlated initial measures propagate. Compare with rule 22 simulations to test loss of low-density effects.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
“Cannot generate randomness intrinsically” depends on the definition of randomness.

The rule 22 contrast is empirical rather than a consequence of additivity.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Rule 90 is left XOR right, so additivity and superposition of the single-cell nested pattern are a short algebraic proof covering every initial condition. The low-density contrast with rule 22 is the same fact read off a simulation and can be reproduced in minutes. The scope is these two rules, which the proof and the runs cover.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Check that rule 90 is linear over GF(2), hence every spacetime diagram is the XOR of single-cell diagrams, and compare a low-density random seed under rule 90 and rule 22. Persistent density modulation in rule 90 and its disappearance in rule 22 confirm the contrast; a nonlinear identity, or a low-density effect that dies in rule 90, would refute the corresponding clause.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The density picture is a finite run; the persistence claim itself follows from linearity.

Cannot generate randomness intrinsically is settled by the superposition theorem, not by a statistical test.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Rule 90 is additive (linear over GF(2)): its local rule is l XOR r, so every evolution is the XOR superposition of shifted copies of the single-cell nested (Pascal mod 2) pattern. Consequently a biased random initial condition leaves a permanent trace: at every time t = 2^k each cell is the XOR of exactly two initial cells, so the density returns to 2p(1-p) forever for initial density p, and the single-cell pattern itself is nested, not random. Rule 22 (non-additive, class 3) instead forgets the initial density: from any initial density the density converges to one common value.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py: (A) checks phi(a XOR b) = phi(a) XOR phi(b) over all 64 neighbourhood pairs for rules 90 and 22; (B) evolves 50 random rows on a 513-cell cyclic lattice for 256 steps under rule 90 and compares every row with the XOR of the single-cell evolution shifted to each initially black cell; (C) counts black cells in the rule-90 single-cell pattern at t = 2^k and 2^k - 1; (D, E) evolve Bernoulli(p) rows of 100000 + 2*1024 cells for 1024 steps under rule 90 (p = 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5) and rule 22 (same p) with zero boundaries, measuring the density in the central 100000 cells, which the boundaries cannot influence within 1024 steps; D compares rule-90 densities at t = 2^k with 2p(1-p), E compares the rule-22 time-averaged densities over t = 512..1024 across p.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. (A) Additivity: the rule-90 local map phi satisfies phi(a XOR b) = phi(a) XOR phi(b) for all 64 pairs of 3-cell neighbourhoods, and the rule-22 map does not; (B) superposition: for 50 random initial conditions on a cyclic lattice of width 513 run for 256 steps, the rule-90 evolution equals the cellwise XOR of the shifted single-cell evolutions exactly (100% of 50*256 rows); (C) single-cell pattern: for rule 90 from one black cell the row at t = 2^k (k = 0..10) has exactly 2 black cells and the row at t = 2^k - 1 has 2^k black cells (nested, Pascal mod 2); (D) persistence in rule 90: with initial densities p in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2} on a measured window of 100000 cells (array padded by 1024 cells on each side so boundaries never reach the window), the measured density at t = 2^k for k = 0..10 is within 0.01 of 2p(1-p) in all 33 cases, and at t = 1024 the three densities differ from the p = 0.5 density by more than 0.1; (E) loss of memory in rule 22: with p in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5} on the same windows, the time-averaged densities over t = 512..1024 differ from one another by less than 0.01 (max minus min). 'Supports' requires A-E.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if A or B fails in any case (rule 90 is not additive / not a superposition), or if in D the rule-90 density at t = 1024 for p = 0.1 lies within 0.05 of the p = 0.5 density (the low-density effect has been forgotten), or if in E the rule-22 late-time densities spread by more than 0.05 (rule 22 remembers the initial density). Other combinations are 'mixed'.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: largest |density(t=2^k) - 2p(1-p)| over p in {0.05,0.1,0.2}, k = 0..10 for rule 90 (threshold 0.01)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: The claim has an algebraic clause (additivity, superposition) and an empirical clause (density persistence in rule 90 versus rule 22, the quoted sentence on p. 265). Additivity is checked exhaustively on the local rule and by exact superposition on random configurations. 'Cannot generate randomness intrinsically' is operationalized by the exact nested structure of the single-cell pattern plus the superposition identity: everything in a rule-90 pattern is a XOR of shifted copies of that nested pattern. 'Low initial density persists forever' is operationalized by the density at times 2^k, where rule 90 reduces to x_t(i) = x_0(i-2^k) XOR x_0(i+2^k) and the density must equal 2p(1-p) at arbitrarily late times; 'no long-term effect' in rule 22 is operationalized as late-time density independent of the initial density. Random initial conditions are Bernoulli(p) with fixed seeds; the lattice is a finite array measured only in a window unaffected by the boundaries within the run length. Rule numbering is Wolfram's standard code (rule 90 = l XOR r; rule 22 = exactly one of l, c, r black).

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Elementary cellular automata 90 and 22 (generated by analysis.py)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Part C initially failed for a trivial reason unrelated to the claim: the single-cell array was two cells too narrow and the fixed-zero boundary cells coincided with the two black cells at t = 1024. The array was widened by one cell on each side (commit history shows the change); no threshold or criterion was changed.

The densities of 100000 cells in one row are correlated (in rule 90 at t = 2^k, cells 2^(k+1) apart share an initial cell), so the binomial standard error (0.0012 for p = 0.1) understates the sampling error; the pre-registered 0.01 tolerance was chosen to absorb this and the largest deviation observed was 0.0031.

Rule 22's late-time density of about 0.351 from all four initial densities agrees with the known asymptotic density of rule 22 from random initial conditions; convergence is complete by t ~ 128 even for p = 0.05.

'Cannot generate randomness intrinsically' is interpreted structurally (every pattern is a superposition of the nested single-cell pattern); whether XOR-superposed nested patterns count as 'random' under some statistical test is not what is being tested. Rule 90 from a p = 0.5 random row does look random and has density 0.5 at all times, consistent with 'randomness from the initial conditions'.

Finite run: 1024 steps and times up to 2^10; 'forever' follows from the identity x_t(i) = x_0(i-2^k) XOR x_0(i+2^k) at t = 2^k, which holds for all k by additivity (verified in A and B), so the finite check is of the mechanism, not a substitute for the proof.
